Mind: bears the service gate and Wren whole, unburned, unexcused, alongside the white dress, Thistle's smile, Marnie's first cry, her laugh and last breath, the bakery, the flour sack, the ash pits, and the water ledgers; distrusts hope as a noose but answered the dark at last ('I'm here' on the 31st day, her first words since the 28th night; the scratching answered back — three slow scratches, a pause, three more — and her first exchange with the woman digging toward her, still unnamed to her, has begun); she waits for the voice to come again. Goal: survive, hold her mind, refuse the hunger, bear the memories without justifying or forgetting, and continue the exchange with the voice when it returns.

On the 32nd day the memory-tide brought the service gate: at sixteen, in the sixth year of the dry season, Vex begged for scraps at the Founders' service gate for about a year and met guard Wren — an older, weary man in patched grey livery with a tin cup and a family below the Quarter — who slipped her bread (a heel in cloth, later rolls in a hollow in the wall), called her 'girl,' never asked her name, and asked only that she make no trouble. Wren was neither enemy nor savior: the hand that turned the key and the hand that slipped the bread, the middleman of the tyranny, the constrained kindness of the ordinary trapped between survival and consent. Vex kept the bread secret and fed Marnie first; she learned to read the city through such tired men. Wren died of the dry cough in the sixth year (replaced by a guard with a face like a closed door); Vex never learned his burial place or name, and saw in him the shape of all the middlemen the fire would later burn — including the younger guard Corin, whose name would be carved into her heart with the dead, and the weary unnamed guard of her imprisonment.

At dawn of the 32nd day Vex set the 32nd stone down in its place in the row along the water channel, spending the day of the service-gate and Wren memory at last. The row now numbers thirty-two, with the fever-gap 27th stone in place; she has still eaten nothing since the 27th. The scratching behind the loose block answered her on the 31st day ('I'm here' / three slow scratches back), and she waits for the voice to come again.

Per the outline, in the years of begging at the Founders' service gate Vex will meet Corin, the younger guard who turns a blind eye to her presence, slips bread occasionally, and warns her not to make trouble — a weary, decent man compromised by the system that feeds him, embodying the constrained kindness she first learned through Wren. Corin and his sister will later die in the Cataclysm; present-day Vex carries his name among the dead.

The exchange with the voice behind the loose block has begun (Vex answered 'I'm here'; the scratching answered back). In a later chapter the voice will speak again directly, and the relationship building toward the block being pushed fully aside and the voice naming herself as Sorrel of the Low Light will continue.

chapters.name: Thistle's Eyes
chapters.content:
On the thirty-third day the memory came up out of the dark like something surfacing, and Vex let it. The drip counted the seconds, the light shaft measured the fall of the morning, and she lay on the stone with the taste of iron and dust and bread in her mouth and let the service gate rise around her whole.

She was sixteen, in the sixth year of the dry season, and she had been coming to the Founders' service gate for a year. Wren had been on the gate then, tired and grey, and Vex had learned to read him the way she had learned to read the fire: by attention, by patience, by the shape of what he would not say.

The day Thistle came into her life was not a special day. It was a morning that felt like every other, the lane grey with dust, the wagons already in, the gate standing open for deliveries. Vex stood at the mouth of the lane in her usual place, out of sight of the guardhouse but well within the smell of bread, waiting for the arrangement to renew itself.

Only the gate was not empty.

A girl was leaning against the gatepost, small and sharp-chinned, younger than Vex by a year or two, with hair the color of wet straw escaping a cap that had once been white. She wore a grey apron gone dark with dishwater, and she was watching Vex the way you watch a thing you have heard about and are now seeing for the first time.

Vex did not move. She had learned not to move when a stranger looked at her. But this girl's eyes were not cruel. They were dark and bright and tired, and there was something in them Vex could not name at first, something quick and crooked, like a door left open in a house where every other door was shut.

"Are you the one they call Vex?" the girl asked. Her voice was a scrape, a laugh buried in it like a splinter under a nail. "The one old Wren feeds?"

Vex felt the heat in her palms rise. She pressed her hands flat against her skirts and forced it down. "He doesn't feed me. He slips me bread. There's a difference."

"Is there?" The girl grinned, quick and crooked and defiant, and Vex understood, in that first heartbeat, that this was a face she would carry for the rest of her life, and that it had entered her chest like a splinter and was already too deep to pull out. "I scrub what the Founders eat off the plates it was served on, and I scrape the bones of their banquets into the slop pail, and the poor eat the scraps and everyone calls it charity." She laughed, cracked at the edges, the laugh of a girl who had learned to laugh before she learned to sleep. "I'm Thistle. Like the weed. The one that grows where nobody wants it and won't die."

"Thistle," Vex repeated, and the name settled into her mouth like a coin dropped into a jar.

"That's me. I've seen you out here every morning for a year, standing in the dust like a kicked dog that keeps coming back because the hand that kicks it also drops a crust sometimes. Wren calls you 'girl' and never asks your name, and the two of you pretend you're not both drowning." She set down her pail and wiped her hands on her apron. "You're not a beggar. Beggars beg. You're waiting for something."

Vex did not answer. She had learned, in the years of wet cloths and ash pits and hidden hands, that the only currency she owned was silence, and she did not spend it on strangers.

Thistle did not seem to mind. She reached into her apron pocket, pulled out a heel of bread still warm, smelling of butter and honey and a life Vex had never touched, and slipped it through the gate the way you slip a coin to a pickpocket.

"Here. Don't eat it here. Old Wren's good, but he's got eyes in the back of his head." She jerked her chin at the guardhouse. "Tomorrow. Same hour. I get out of the kitchens at the bell. Bring me news from the lower districts—what the wells are doing, who's sick, whether the water cart came through, what the board's been posting. I get tired of hearing about Founders' business. I want to hear about the real city for once."

Vex took the bread. It had been slipped to her, not thrown, and the weight of it was heavier than the weight of Wren's bread, as if it had cost the girl more than a heel of bread to give.

"Why me?" Vex asked.

Thistle looked at her, and for a moment the grin was gone, and the face underneath was bare and tired and old in a way that had nothing to do with years.

"Because you're the only one out here who looks back. Everyone else in the lane looks at their feet. You look at the gate, at the guards, at me. You look like you're counting something. Like you're keeping score." She picked up her pail. "I like people who keep score. The Founders keep score. Someone ought to keep score on them."

She went through the gate, and the gate swung shut behind her, and Vex stood in the lane with the warm bread in her hands and the splinter in her chest and understood that the arrangement had changed. There were two hands slipping her bread now, and one of them belonged to a girl who kept score.

The friendship grew the way things grow in poor soil: thin, crooked, alive.

Every morning at the bell, before the Founders' dinner, Thistle came out through the service gate with her pail and her apron and her crooked smile, and Vex came to the mouth of the lane, and they stood in the dust by the wall where the guards could not see them and traded the city back and forth like two girls trading stolen raisins, piece by piece.

Vex brought the news she had been asked for. She told Thistle about the wells shrinking, the east well gone brown, the mothers standing in line at the cistern gate with their ration tokens and their thin arms. She told her about the healer's door in the lower districts shut for a week, and the cough moving through the children like a rumor, and the way the public board had posted a new proclamation about "providential thrift" over the ration notices, as if the sky had decided the poor should drink less.

Thistle listened with her whole body, leaning in, her dark bright tired eyes fixed on Vex's face as if the news were water and she had been thirsty for years.

"Providential thrift," she repeated once, low, a blade wrapped in a laugh. "You hear that? They've decided hunger is a virtue. They sit in their Quarter with their full cisterns and their banquet menus, and they sleep well at night, every one of them, because they've built their beds out of our silence. We die quietly, Vex. That's the whole trick of it. We die quietly, and they sleep."

In return, Thistle gave Vex the only thing a scullery maid had to give: the inside of the beast.

She told Vex about the Founders' kitchens—the ovens that ran all day, the pantries stocked with things the lower districts had not seen in years, the ice cellar carved into the hill where they kept the cream for the banquet desserts. She told her about the Founders' daughters who rang for more hot water and let it cool; about the steward who weighed the flour every morning and counted the loaves every night and had never once gone hungry. She told her about the dinner menus, course by course, as if reciting a litany: quail in honey, wine-glazed pheasant, a cream served in cups of cistern ice.

"The cups," Thistle said once, and her voice was strange, almost wondering. "They serve the cream in cups carved out of the ice. They drink cold things because they can, because the ice is theirs. And down in the lane, the children are dying of thirst, and no one ever makes them look."

The small rebellions were Thistle's idea.

The first was almost nothing: a single Founders' loaf, taken from the evening bake before it could be counted, smuggled out in the slop pail under a layer of dishwater and delivered to a family Vex knew was hungry. It was a crime, small and bright, and it was the first time Vex had stolen anything and not felt its weight.

"See?" Thistle whispered, crouched by the wall, grinning her crooked grin. "That's the thing they don't understand. They think the slop pail is full of garbage. They never look inside. They never look at anything they think is beneath them. That's the crack."

After that came the loosened bolt on a water cart, one afternoon, so that a stream of the Quarter's own water ran out into the dust of the service lane and soaked into the ground before anyone noticed, and the lane smelled of wet earth for a day, and the children of the lower districts came and pressed their hands to the damp and would not let go. Thistle did that one alone, and came back with her apron soaked and her eyes bright and her hands shaking, and she laughed, cracked and defiant, and said: "They'll never know. They'll think a pipe burst. Let them think it."

Vex brought the news, and Thistle made the mischief, and between them grew the thing neither of them named: a conspiracy, small and crooked and alive, two girls keeping score on the Founders with stolen bread and loosened bolts and whispered news, doing the only damage they could do, which was to refuse to die quietly.

And once, in the stolen half-hour before the Founders' dinner, standing in the market square where the public board held a Founder's painted face up to the crowd, Thistle told Vex her dream.

It came out the way water comes out of a nearly dry well: slow, and with effort, as if she had been carrying it a long time and had only just decided to set it down.

"The sea," she said, looking past the crowd, past the board, past the city, at something Vex could not see. "Have you seen the sea, Vex? I haven't. But I've heard. Water everywhere. Water falling from the sky for free, for everyone, no permits, no buckets, no Founders with their hands out. Rain. Can you imagine? Standing in it, open-mouthed, and no one to tell you to pay."

Vex could not imagine it. The sky over Meridian was a locked cistern of its own, and she had learned not to want what it would not give.

"When the Founders feel the hunger," Thistle went on, quiet now, the grin gone, "I'm going to walk out of this city with my wages in a knot in my apron and walk until I can stand under a sky that doesn't owe me a drop. You can come. You can see the sea."

And Vex stood in the market square with the heat in her palms and the Founder's painted mouth above her and wanted, with a wanting that frightened her, to tell the girl what slept under her scars. The words were there, the whole confession—the ash pits, the flour sack, the unburned palms, the fire that answered her will like a dog answering a whistle. Thistle was looking at her with those dark bright tired eyes, and there was nothing in them that would have flinched.

But she did not say it. The crowd applauded the portrait, Thistle's grin came back, quick and crooked, and she went back to the kitchens, and Vex stood in the square with the heat in her palms and the secret in her chest and the splinter going deeper, and she told herself the lie she would tell for years: that the fire was hers alone, that keeping it secret was a kind of protection.

The truth, which she would not know until much later, lying on the stone of a tear-shaped cell with the drip counting out the days, was that Thistle already knew.

Not the fact of it. Thistle did not know about the ash pits or the flour sack or the hands that never burned. But she knew something was there. She had known it from the first morning at the gate, when she had looked at Vex standing in the dust and seen, behind the beggar's stillness, a girl who was waiting for something, a girl who was keeping score.

"You've got something in you," Thistle said once, near the end, in the stolen hour by the wall, her head tilted, her eyes narrowed, not afraid, curious, drawn. "I don't know what it is. I don't want to know. But it's not bread, and it's not patience, and it's not the kind of waiting I do. You're not waiting for a door to open, Vex. You're waiting for a door to break."

Vex's hands went flat against her skirts, the heat rising, forced down.

"Whatever it is," Thistle said, and her voice was low and serious now, the laugh gone, "when it comes—promise me they'll feel it. Promise me we won't die quietly."

And Vex, sixteen, with heat in her palms and a sister dying of locked water and a ledger building in her skull, looked at the scullery maid through the bars of the gate and said:

"I promise."

The memory broke there, the way memories broke, and Vex lay on the cold stone of the oubliette with the drip going on and the dark pressing in, and she held the shape of Thistle's eyes in her chest: dark and bright and tired, the eyes of a girl who had seen her, who had known, in her way, exactly what was sleeping under the scars, and had been drawn to it anyway. That was the terrible thing: Thistle had seen the danger in her and had not turned away. Thistle had leaned in. Thistle had handed her the bread and the dream and the promise, and Vex had kept the secret, and the secret had burned her alive.

She had told Thistle nothing of the fire. She had thought she was protecting her, building a wall between the girl she loved and the hunger with her name on it. And in the end the hunger had eaten through the wall and the girl together, because the fire did not discriminate and the ledger would not balance and the beast she had released had its own appetite.

Vex pressed her palms to the stone, and the heat in them stirred, and she let it, and then, deliberately, forced it down. She was not going to burn the memory. She had tried that on the twenty-seventh day and learned the heat was a hunger that fed on memory, not a cautery. Thistle's smile was the one thing the fire could not eat. Thistle's eyes were the one thing in the whole burned city that would not turn to ash.

She held them instead. She held the dark bright tired eyes, and the quick crooked defiant grin, and the voice scraped thin by years of dishwater, and the dream of the sea, and the rain falling on everyone, and the promise she had made and broken and made again in the burning yard, and she did not justify it and she did not forget it and she did not try to make it balance. She let it be what it was: the first thing that had ever seen her whole, and the price of everything that came after.

The light shaft paled. Dawn of the thirty-third day, and Vex crawled to the water channel and set down the thirty-third stone, adding it to the row with her raw fingers. Thirty-three stones. The bowls still stood untouched in the corner; the hunger was a presence in her now, patient as the drip, and she did not eat, because the choice was hers, and it was the one thing in the cell that was hers.

She lay back on the stone and closed her eyes, and the dark behind the loose block in the wall held its breath, patient as the drip, patient as the woman digging toward her. The exchange had begun on the thirty-first day—I'm here, and the scratching answering back—and the voice had not come again, not yet, but it would. It had promised. It was digging.

Vex thought of Thistle's eyes, and of the girl who had seen the danger in her and leaned in anyway, and of the woman on the other side of the wall who had heard her screaming in the dark and had not turned away, and she understood that the woman digging toward her was of a piece with the girl at the gate: someone who had looked at her and decided, against all the arithmetic of the city, to keep looking.

The drip went on. The light shaft paled. Somewhere above, the festival was building toward the first of the harvest month, toward the pyre, toward her—and the girl who had once kept her secret from a scullery maid, and lost her to the hunger the secret fed, was learning, at last, that the only way to carry the dead was to carry them whole: unburned, unexcused, and unforgotten.

She held Thistle's eyes in her chest like a hand over a candle, and let them be the tenderest truth she owned, and waited for whatever was coming to come.

set.name: Vex
set.description: Young woman, former baker's apprentice of Meridian, condemned for the Cataclysm fire. Imprisoned in the tear-shaped oubliette beneath the old courthouse, below the city's waterline, awaiting public immolation at the Sanctum square on the first day of the harvest festival (festival banners up; crowds gathering; wood stacked). The 33rd day is under way: at dawn she set the 33rd stone in its place in the row along the water channel; the row now numbers thirty-three, with the fever-gap 27th stone in place; her day-marking ritual continues. On the 33rd day the memory-tide brought Thistle's eyes — her first full encounter with Thistle at the Founders' service gate, when Vex was sixteen in the sixth year of the dry season, while Wren was still on the gate: Thistle (a year or two younger, sharp-chinned, hair the color of wet straw escaping a cap that had once been white, grey apron dark with dishwater, dark bright tired eyes, a quick crooked defiant grin, a laugh cracked at the edges) slipped her a heel of bread through the gate, named herself ('Thistle. Like the weed. The one that grows where nobody wants it and won't die.'), and arranged daily stolen meetings at the bell: Vex brought news from the lower districts (shrinking wells, the shut healer's door, the cough among children, the board's 'providential thrift'), Thistle gave her the inside of the Founders' kitchens (all-day ovens, ice cellar, seven-course menus recited as a litany, the Founders who sleep well because the poor die quietly). They conspired in small rebellions: a Founders' loaf smuggled out in the slop pail under dishwater; a loosened bolt on a water cart letting the Quarter's own water soak the service lane while the children pressed their hands to the damp. In a stolen half-hour in the market square, Thistle shared her dream of the sea — water falling from the sky for free, no permits, no buckets, no Founders with their hands out — and invited Vex to come. Thistle sensed the danger sleeping in Vex ('You're not waiting for a door to open, Vex. You're waiting for a door to break.') and was drawn to it, not afraid, and made Vex promise: 'Promise me they'll feel it. Promise me we won't die quietly.' Vex promised. She never told Thistle about the fire, believing secrecy was protection; she now understands Thistle saw the danger and leaned in anyway, that the secret was a wall the hunger later ate through along with the girl, and that Thistle's eyes are the one thing in the burned city that will not turn to ash — she holds the memory whole, unburned, unexcused, alongside Wren, the white dress, Marnie, the bakery, the ash pits, and the water ledgers. Physical: fever long broken; weak and starving — has eaten nothing since the 27th (the morning and evening bowls of the 27th and 28th still untouched in the corner); drank a little from the fresh jug; hunger now a patient presence, quieter than the fire; voice a rasp but she is speaking again; torn fingernails, palms raw and bloodied over the pale scars 'the handles,' knees raw from kneeling, long bruise along her left side, stiff sweat-dried shift, matted hair; the trial's gag cut the corners of her mouth. Mind: distrusts hope as a noose but answered the dark at last ('I'm here' on the 31st day; the scratching answered back — three slow scratches, a pause, three more); she waits for the voice behind the loose block (still unnamed to her) to speak again; she understands the woman digging toward her is of a piece with Thistle — someone who looked at her and decided, against the city's arithmetic, to keep looking. Goal: survive, hold her mind, refuse the hunger, bear the memories without justifying or forgetting, and continue the exchange with the voice when it returns.

On the 33rd day in the oubliette, the memory-tide brought Vex's first full encounter with Thistle at the Founders' service gate, when Vex was sixteen in the sixth year of the dry season while Wren was still on the gate: Thistle, a younger scullery maid with wet-straw hair, a once-white cap, and dark bright tired eyes, slipped her a heel of warm bread through the gate, named herself ('like the weed that grows where nobody wants it'), and arranged daily stolen meetings trading Vex's news from the lower districts for Thistle's news of the Founders' kitchens.

Vex's friendship with Thistle grew through small conspiracies against the Founders' order: a Founders' loaf smuggled out in the slop pail, a loosened bolt on a water cart letting water soak the service lane, whispered news traded at the bell. Thistle shared her dream of the sea where water falls from the sky for free, sensed the dangerous thing sleeping in Vex ('You're not waiting for a door to open. You're waiting for a door to break') and was drawn to it, and made Vex promise: 'Promise me they'll feel it. Promise me we won't die quietly.' Vex promised and never told her about the fire — a secret that became, in the end, a wall the hunger ate through along with Thistle herself.

At dawn of the 33rd day Vex set the 33rd stone down in its place in the row along the water channel, spending the day of the Thistle memory at last. The row now numbers thirty-three, with the fever-gap 27th stone in place; she has still eaten nothing since the 27th. She holds Thistle's eyes whole, unburned, unexcused, and waits for the voice behind the loose block to speak again.

The bond between Vex and Thistle, established at the service gate (the bread, the dream of the sea, the promise that they will not die quietly), continues to deepen across subsequent memories. The memory-tide carries Vex forward from the gate toward the next milestone of the past: the Founders' seven-course banquet menu posted on the public board in the sixth year of the dry season — the point of no return where her rage crystallizes, immediately before Marnie's sickness and death. Thistle's dream and Vex's promise will collide with that rage in the chapters ahead.

The woman digging toward Vex behind the loose block (still unnamed to Vex; to prove to be Sorrel of the Low Light, Thistle's sister) has not yet spoken again since Vex answered 'I'm here' on the 31st day. In a later chapter the voice will speak again directly, and the relationship building toward the block being pushed fully aside and the voice naming herself as Sorrel — who knows Thistle, the service gate, and the bread — will continue.

chapters.name: The Banquet Menu
chapters.content:
On the thirty-fourth day the memory came up out of the dark the way heat comes off a coal — slow, then all at once — and Vex let it. The drip counted, the light shaft measured, and she lay on the stone with the taste of ash in her mouth and let the sixth year of the dry season rise around her whole.

It was the month the Founders posted the menu.

Vex had read the public board for as long as she could read — which was to say, for as long as her mother had dared teach her, between prayers, with a burnt stick on a slate. The board was the city's one true tongue: the price of bread, the hour of curfew, the size of the ration, the name of the saint the Order burned candles to this week. It told you what you were allowed to know.

And on that morning, in the sixth year of the dry season, when the east well had gone brown and the children of the lower districts stood in the gutter watching the water carts roll past without stopping, the board told them about dinner.

The Founders had posted their banquet menu.

Vex remembered the ink. That was the first thing that came back — fresh, black, lavish, laid down in letters twice the size of the ration notice it had been pasted over, as if the menu had eaten the board the way the Founders ate everything. She remembered the crowd, the silence of it, a silence with a shape, like a held breath. A woman at her elbow was crying without a sound, tears running straight into the dust, and no one looked at her, because everyone was looking at the board.

QUAIL IN HONEY, the board said. WINE-GLAZED PHEASANT. CREAM IN CUPS OF CISTERN ICE. Seven courses for one dinner, and at the bottom, in the same lavish hand: IN HONOR OF THE FOUNDING, THE FOUNDERS INVITE THE CITY TO REJOICE IN THE BOUNTY OF THE PROVINCE.

The province that had not seen rain in six years. Thistle had recited this menu to her once, in the dust by the service gate, as a litany. Thistle had scraped the bones of that dinner into a slop pail. And here it was now, printed, public, hung over the ration notices like a flag over a conquered town.

Vex read the menu twice. The first time she read it as the board wanted to be read — a promise of abundance, a celebration. The second time she read it the way Thistle had taught her to read everything the Founders wrote: as a confession.

The menu was not an invitation. It was a ledger. The Founders were not telling the city what they would eat; they were telling the city what the city could not have. Seven courses, and the east well brown, and the ration line around the block, and a mother somewhere selling her wedding ring for a bucket of brackish water. Beneath it, half-covered by fresh paste, the ration notice: the lower districts would receive less this month, in keeping with providential thrift.

Something in Vex's chest — something that had been a coal for years, banked under wet cloths and prayers and the habit of staying small — caught, and glowed.

She stood very still in the crowd and let it happen. She did not move, did not speak, did not let the heat into her palms where anyone could see. But she felt the shape of the coal change. All her life the heat had been shame — a crack in the orderly world, a heresy to bind and pray over. Standing before the board, she felt it become something else. A fact. The Founders had written it down themselves, in ink, where the poor could read: this is what we have, and this is what you are not. The menu was cruelty by design, posted like a gauntlet, and the city had taken it the way it took everything — quietly.

We die quietly, Thistle had said. That's the whole trick of it. We die quietly, and they sleep.

Vex turned away from the board and went home.

The memory shifted, and suddenly she was in the bakery, and the first wrongness was the silence.

Marnie was never silent. Marnie was six years old and the world was a question and she asked it at full volume from the moment she woke, her quick crooked laugh ringing off the flour sacks like a bell that had never learned the curfew. Instead the bakery was quiet, and the quiet was the worst sound Vex had ever heard, because it was Marnie-shaped, a hole in the air where the laugh should have been.

Their mother stood at the back room's door with her hands gone grey in the dough she had stopped kneading, and the shape of her face said it all.

"Don't come in," she said. "Vex. I think it's the —"

But Vex was already past her, already at the pallet, already on her knees.

Marnie lay on the straw with her small dark hair plastered to her forehead and her eyes half-open, and she was burning. Vex had carried heat in her hands all her life and knew the feel of it, the live trembling weight of it, and Marnie's skin was doing something that had nothing to do with fire — a fever with its own wet shine, its own rattling breath. The dry cough that Vex had told herself was nothing, was the dust, was the season, had become a thing with a voice. Marnie's belly, the hunger-bloom swelling all year, lay hard and tight under the flour-sack tunic, her lips cracked, and her eyes, when they found Vex's face, were the same frank fearless eyes that had looked at her in the first hour of her life — but tired now, tired in a way no six-year-old should know.

"Vex," Marnie whispered. The word came out dry, a rustle. "I'm thirsty."

That was the word that broke Vex open. Not the fever, not the rattling breath, not the tight belly — the word thirsty, said by a child who had never once been told she could not have the raisins, said in the voice of a child asking for the thing the whole city was built to deny her. Vex stood up, her hands steady, the coal in her chest glowing, and went out to find water.

The search for mercy took her through the whole lower city, and the memory gave it to her in pieces, a mosaic of shut doors.

She went to the healer's door first. A small door at the end of a crooked lane, with a painted hand over it that had once meant help, shut, and shut for a week. When Vex hammered on it with both fists, the silence on the other side had a shape, the same shape as the silence of the crowd at the board. Finally a voice came through the wood — a daughter's, thin and ashamed and final. "He's gone to the Quarter. He doesn't cross the line anymore. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry." And the shame made it worse, because the girl meant it, and meaning it did not open the door.

Vex went to the cistern gate.

The cistern gate was the iron heart of the lower districts' long dying, and Vex knew it by heart: the bars, the lock, the clerk in Founders' grey at a folding table with the ration ledger open, the line of mothers with their tokens, the water cart at the head of the line, full, going nowhere, going to the Quarter. Vex had no token. The ration had been cut again, in keeping with providential thrift.

"My sister is sick," Vex said. "She's six. She needs water. Clean water. Please."

The clerk did not look up. "Token."

"She's burning up. She can't —"

"Token," the clerk said again, and the word was a door, and it shut.

Vex stood at the iron gate and looked at the water — blessed, ordinary, impossible, standing in the cart in full view, enough to save every child in the district — and understood, with a clarity like a blade going in, that the water was not water anymore. It was a wall. Some are chosen to drink, some are chosen to thirst, and the thirst is holy, and the hoarding is order, and the dying is providential.

She went to the Order.

The chapel of the Chastened Flame stood at the district's edge with its censers and its candles — permitted fire, holy fire, fire that burned only what it was given — and the priest stood on the step with his hands folded in the approved posture of sorrow, and Vex knelt on the stones and said the words she had been taught, the words that were supposed to open the sky: "Please. My sister has the Flux. She needs water, and the gate is shut, and the healer won't come. What do I do?"

The priest looked at her, and she saw it in his face: he did not know. He had no water and no answer and no power, and what he had instead was the doctrine, and he gave it to her the way the Order gave everything to the poor — in place of what they needed.

"Thirst is the test," he said, gently, kindly, with real sorrow in his voice, as if sorrow were a bucket. "The Chastened Flame refines what it burns. Your sister's suffering is —"

Vex stood up in the middle of the priest's sentence, and the coal in her chest caught, and for one heartbeat the heat rose into her hands and she wanted — oh, she wanted — to hold her palm over the censer and let the flame bend around her skin and ask him which of them it was refining. But Marnie was waiting. Marnie was thirsty. Vex turned and walked away, and the censers burned their permitted flame, and the sky did not open, and nothing changed.

The memory gave her the rest in a blur of running: the water carts rolling past without stopping, the brown water of the east well she could not give a child with the Flux, the mothers in the ration line turning their faces away because to look at her was to look at their own children's tomorrows. She ran until her lungs burned, and the coal burned with a different heat, and at every shut door and iron bar and folded hand she heard the city's answer to her sister's thirst, the same answer in a hundred costumes: not our problem. Providential. Ordered. Holy. Quiet.

Night fell. The Founders' banquet music floated over the walls of the Quarter — strings and horns, a waltz, something bright and ignorant — while the lower districts lay in the dark and listened, the way they had listened for six years.

Vex came back to the bakery empty-handed.

Their mother had done what she could — a wet rag on Marnie's forehead, a cup of brackish well-water held to the cracked lips, Marnie coughing it back up in a thin brown stream — and she sat by the pallet with her grey face and folded hands, praying the prayer that had never once filled a bucket. Vex knelt on the other side of the pallet and took her sister's hand.

Marnie's eyes opened. The fever had her now, really had her, and for a moment there was no recognition in them, only heat and thirst and the small animal struggle of a body losing its water. Then the eyes found Vex's face, and recognition came back, and Marnie smiled — the quick crooked delighted smile, the smile that had never learned the curfew — and whispered, "You came back. You'll fix it. You always fix it."

And Vex, sixteen years old, with the heat lying in her palms like a sleeping thing and the coal in her chest gone white-hot and the banquet music drifting over the walls, looked at her sister and understood the shape of her own life at last.

The Founders were not merely cruel.

That was the thought that came to her, clean and terrible, while she held her sister's burning hand. Cruelty was a sin, and sins could be repented, and the city could pray over its sins and go on. The Founders were not cruel. They were a disease — a fever in the body of the city, a flux of the spirit that had learned to call itself order, that fed on the thirsty and slept well and posted its menus where the starving could read them. Cruelty was a choice a man made. A disease was a thing that grew, that spread, that consumed, that had to be —

cauterized.

Something inside her knew how to cauterize.

She had known it since the ash pits, since the flour sack, since the first time she had set a dry leaf alight with a thought and watched the flame answer her will like a dog answering a whistle. All her life she had called it shame, bound it in wet cloths, hidden it behind her back, whispered prayers over it — because the Order said fire was heresy, because her mother said stay small, because Thistle had seen it sleeping in her and leaned in anyway, because Marnie had named it magic and pressed it to her cheek without fear. And all her life it had been waiting — patient as the drip, patient as the wanting — for the day she stopped calling it shame and called it by its true name.

The Founders were a disease. And she was the cautery.

Vex sat on the floor of the bakery with her sister's fever burning under her hand and the banquet music floating over the walls, and she did not speak the resolution aloud. It was not a plan yet; it was a coal taking shape in her chest, glowing through the wet cloths and the prayers and the staying small, and she held it the way she held her sister's hand, and she knew, with the same terrible clarity, that it would not be banked again.

Somewhere above, the Founders drank their cream from cups of cistern ice. Somewhere below, her sister burned with thirst. And in between, Vex sat in the dark and let the resolution take its shape, and the shape it took was the shape of a door she had been waiting all her life to break.

The memory broke there, the way memories broke, and Vex lay on the cold stone of the oubliette with the drip going on and the dark pressing in, and she held the coal in her chest — the coal that had become the Cataclysm, that had burned Thistle and the white dress and the Foundling child and the laundress and the cook's boy and the debtors, that had made her the monster the city needed and the liberator the city whispered to in the ashes. She did not justify it. She had stopped trying to justify it on the twenty-seventh day, when she had learned that the ledger would not balance and no arithmetic of the Founders' crimes would make Thistle's death weigh less. But she could bear it. That was what the row of stones had taught her: to take the memories whole, unburned, unexcused — even this one, the memory of the exact moment the fire stopped being a shame and became a choice.

The memory of the point of no return.

Vex pressed her palms to the stone, and the heat in them stirred, and she let it, and then deliberately forced it down. She was not going to feed the coal; she had learned that hunger, too. She lay in the dark with the banquet menu printed behind her eyes — quail in honey, wine-glazed pheasant, cream in cups of cistern ice — and with Marnie's dry voice saying I'm thirsty, and she held them both the way she held everything now: whole, unburned, unexcused, unforgotten. She did not need to decide again. She had decided, in that bakery, in the sixth year of the dry season, and the decision had burned the world, and she was learning now, at the bottom of a tear-shaped cell with the festival building toward the pyre, that the only way to carry the decision was to carry it whole, and to keep looking at it, and not to look away.

The light shaft paled. Dawn of the thirty-fourth day, and Vex crawled to the water channel and set down the thirty-fourth stone, adding it to the row with her raw fingers. Thirty-four stones. The bowls still stood untouched in the corner; the hunger was a presence in her now, patient as the drip, and she did not eat, because the choice was hers, and it was the one thing in the cell that was hers.

She lay back on the stone and closed her eyes. Somewhere behind the loose block in the wall, the dark held its breath, patient as the drip, patient as the woman digging toward her, patient as the voice that had not spoken again since she had said I'm here — but it would. It had promised. It was digging.

And somewhere above, the festival was building toward the first of the harvest month, toward the pyre, toward her — and the girl who had once stood before a banquet menu and felt her rage crystallize into a coal, who had once held her sister's fever in her hands and named the Founders a disease, was waiting, at last, to find out whether the cautery she had become could ever learn to burn for something other than vengeance.

She held the memory of her sister's thirst in her chest like a hand over a candle, and let it be the tenderest truth she owned, and waited for whatever was coming to come.

set.name: Vex
set.description: Young woman, former baker's apprentice of Meridian, condemned for the Cataclysm fire. Imprisoned in the tear-shaped oubliette beneath the old courthouse, below the city's waterline, awaiting public immolation at the Sanctum square on the first day of the harvest festival (festival banners up; crowds gathering; wood stacked). The 34th day is under way: at dawn she set the 34th stone in its place in the row along the water channel; the row now numbers thirty-four, with the fever-gap 27th stone in place; her day-marking ritual continues. On the 34th day the memory-tide brought the point of no return in the sixth year of the dry season, when Vex was sixteen: the Founders posted their seven-course banquet menu on the public board (quail in honey, wine-glazed pheasant, cream in cups of cistern ice) in letters twice the size of the ration notice, in honor of the Founding, while the east well had gone brown and children stood in the gutter watching water carts roll past. Vex read it twice — first as celebration, then as a confession, a ledger of what the city could not have — and felt her rage crystallize into a coal in her chest, no longer shame but a fact. Returning home she found Marnie, six, sick: fever, dehydration, the hunger-bloom belly hard and tight, lips cracked, the dry cough that Vex had told herself was nothing deepened into a rattling breath, the beginning of the Flux; Marnie's word 'I'm thirsty' broke Vex open. Vex searched the whole lower city for mercy and found none: the healer's door shut (his daughter's thin ashamed voice through the wood — he doesn't cross the district line), the cistern gate clerk refusing her without a token while the full water cart stood at the head of the line, the Order's priest kneeling her and offering the doctrine 'Thirst is the test' / providential thrift in place of water (she wanted to hold her palm over the censer and ask which of them the flame was refining, but Marnie was waiting). Night fell with the Founders' banquet waltz floating over the walls while Marnie coughed up brown brackish well-water. Kneeling by the pallet, holding her sister's fevered hand, Vex understood: the Founders are not merely cruel — cruelty is a sin that can be repented — they are a disease, a fever in the body of the city that feeds on the thirsty and sleeps well, and a disease must be cauterized, and something inside her knows how to cauterize. The resolution took shape in her chest like a coal, no longer to be banked: the point of no return, the moment the fire stopped being a shame and became a choice. She did not speak it aloud; it was not yet a plan. In the present she held the memory whole, unburned, unexcused, unforgotten — including the knowledge that this coal became the Cataclysm that burned Thistle, the white dress, the Foundling child, the laundress, the cook's boy, the debtors — and refused to feed it, forcing the heat down. Physical: fever long broken; weak and starving — has eaten nothing since the 27th (the morning and evening bowls of the 27th and 28th still untouched in the corner); drank a little from the fresh jug; hunger now a patient presence, quieter than the fire; voice a rasp but she is speaking again; torn fingernails, palms raw and bloodied over the pale scars 'the handles,' knees raw from kneeling, long bruise along her left side, stiff sweat-dried shift, matted hair; the trial's gag cut the corners of her mouth. Mind: distrusts hope as a noose but answered the dark at last ('I'm here' on the 31st day; the scratching answered back — three slow scratches, a pause, three more); she waits for the voice behind the loose block (still unnamed to her; to prove to be Sorrel of the Low Light, Thistle's sister) to speak again; she understands the woman digging toward her is of a piece with Thistle — someone who looked at her and decided, against the city's arithmetic, to keep looking. Goal: survive, hold her mind, refuse the hunger, bear the memories without justifying or forgetting — now including the memory of her own resolution, the coal that became the fire — and continue the exchange with the voice when it returns.

That night the Founders' banquet waltz floated over the walls while Marnie coughed up brown brackish well-water.

Kneeling by Marnie's pallet in the sixth year of the dry season, holding her sister's fevered hand, Vex reached her point of no return: she understood the Founders are not merely cruel (cruelty is a sin that can be repented) but a disease in the body of the city, a fever that feeds on the thirsty and sleeps well — and a disease must be cauterized, and something inside her knows how to cauterize. The resolution took shape in her chest like a coal, not yet a plan, never to be banked again: the moment her fire stopped being shame and became a choice.

At dawn of the 34th day Vex set the 34th stone down in its place in the row along the water channel, spending the day of the banquet-menu, Marnie's sickness, and the cautery-resolution memory at last. The row now numbers thirty-four, with the fever-gap 27th stone in place; she has still eaten nothing since the 27th. She held the memory whole and refused to feed the coal, forcing the heat down.

The banquet-menu memory and Marnie's worsening Flux sickness establish the immediate run toward the next milestone of the past: Marnie's death in Vex's arms on the Night of the Wake — the Flux sweeping the lower districts while the Founders' healers serve the rich, the locked cisterns, the healer's door shut, Marnie's rattling final breath, the fire surfacing unbidden in Vex's grief (burning bed and curtains), the silent funeral, and the Founders' banquet music floating over the walls as Vex's childhood ends. The memory-tide will carry Vex to that night in the chapters ahead.

The cautery-resolution coal formed in Vex's chest — the Founders are a disease and something inside her knows how to cauterize — is the point of no return that seeds the Cataclysm: the night Vex leaves the bakery after her mother has gone to bed, walks through the moonlit lower districts, pauses at the gates of the Founders' Quarter with smoking hands, and lifts her palms to the iron gate to let the furnace wake. Future chapters carry this resolution from the bakery floor to the gates.

chapters.name: The Night of the Wake
chapters.content:
On the thirty-fifth day the memory came before the light did, and Vex knew, with the certainty of a hand closing on a known handle, that there was no way to refuse it and no way to prepare for it. Some memories she had met as battles, and some as ledgers, and some as prayers that broke in her mouth. This one she met as an appointment kept. The drip counted. The dark held its breath. And the sixth year of the dry season opened under her and took her down whole.

It was the week the Flux swept the warrens.

The lower districts had been dying of thirst for six years and had learned to do it quietly, but the Flux was not thirst. The Flux came up out of the east wells, where the water had gone brown and then had gone bad, and it did not wait for permission or providential thrift. It took the children first, because children were the thinnest vessels, and then it took the old, and then it took anyone who drank the brown water out of love and had no choice. In the district below the tannery the bells had rung for the nonsense of a funeral every day for a week, and the Founders' healers, who had never crossed the line, did not cross it now. The ration notices did not mention it. The public board posted nothing about the dying, because the public board posted only what the Founders wanted the city to know, and the Founders wanted the city to know about dinner.

In the bakery, Marnie lay on the straw pallet and burned, and Vex sat beside her through the nights with a wet rag and the prayer her mother had taught her, and the prayer did not fill a bucket and the rag did not break the fever and the coal in her chest did not cool.

Vex did not sleep. That was the shape of it, the whole of it, the days and nights running together like brown water into a drain. She left the bakery only to beg, and she begged at every door the city owned. She went back to the cistern gate and stood in the ration line without a token, and the clerk waved her away, and she went to the healer's door and hammered until her fists bled, and the daughter's thin voice through the wood said the same thing it had said before, he doesn't cross the line, I'm sorry, I'm so sorry, and the sorry was a door and it was shut. She went to the service gate of the Founders' Quarter, where the new guard with the face like a closed door stood with his pike, and she dropped to her knees on the cobbles and put her forehead down and begged — begged, the word scraping up out of her like a thing with hooks — for water, for a healer, for a scrap, for anything, and the guard looked through her the way the city looked through her, and the Founders' kitchens went on cooking behind the wall.

It was Wren's old gate. The hollow in the wall where Wren had slipped her bread was empty, and Wren was dead of the dry cough in a year the city had decided not to grieve, and the kindness that had lived in that hollow had died with him.

Somewhere on the third night — or the fourth, she had lost the count — Vex stole. She stole because stealing was all that was left, because begging had failed and the law was on the side of the owners of water. She crept to the Founders' Quarter after curfew, over the wall where the old drain ran dry, and into a stable yard where the horses got what the children could not have, and she filled a leather bottle from the trough and ran, and the water in the bottle was clean and cold and it had cost her everything she had left of the small girl who had never stolen anything but raisins. She held the bottle against her chest all the way home like a stolen heart.

Marnie drank. Vex held the bottle to her sister's cracked lips and Marnie drank, and some of it stayed down, and Vex saw the flicker of hope move across her own chest like a hand testing a door, and the hope was worse than despair because despair had nowhere to go and hope did. She sponged Marnie's burning forehead. She whispered the prayer. She held her sister's small hand and watched the fever hold its ground, and in the grey hour of the fourth night Marnie opened her eyes and looked at her.

"Vex," Marnie said. Her voice was a rustle now, a dry leaf. "Are we going to the sea?"

The word caught Vex in the chest. The sea — Marnie's dream, the sea that has no gates and gives water to everyone, the sea she had spun into night stories out of nothing, out of the ration and the dust and the closed doors. Vex had promised her once, in the warm years, that they would go. She had believed it, in the warm years.

"Soon," Vex said. "When you're better. We'll go to the sea."

Marnie smiled — the quick crooked delighted smile, or the ghost of it — and her eyes were the same frank fearless eyes that had looked at Vex in the first hour of her life, and she said, "You'll fix it. You always fix it."

And Vex held the stolen water in a leather bottle and the coal in her chest and the whole weight of the city on her back, and she answered, "I will. I'll fix it. Sleep now."

Marnie slept. And in the hour before dawn, with her mother asleep in the corner of the bakery, worn out by kneeling, the fever that had been holding its ground closed its hand.

Vex felt it happen. She was holding Marnie's hand, and there was a moment — one heartbeat, no more — when the small fingers that had always found hers went slack, and the rattling breath that had been going on for days, the terrible rhythm Vex had learned to live inside like a tide, simply stopped. Marnie's chest did not rise. Her eyes were open — fixed on Vex's face, the way they had been fixed on Vex's face in the first hour of her life, and the way they would be fixed on it in every hour Vex would ever own again — and the frank fearless trust in them was still there, unspent, waiting for the fixing that had not come.

"You always fix it."

Vex said her name. She said it once, quietly, the way you say a name to wake someone, and then she said it again, and then she was screaming it, and the screaming came up out of her not through her mouth but through her hands.

The fire surfaced unbidden.

Later — in the trial, in the oubliette, in every sleepless hour of the third act of her life — Vex would try to find the exact shape of that moment, the hinge on which it had turned, and she would never find it. There was no intention in it. She had not reached for the heat; the heat had reached for her. It came up out of her grief the way the Flux had come up out of the wells, a thing with its own appetite, and it took the straw pallet first. The straw caught with a sound like a sharp intake of breath, and the flame ran up the bedclothes and took the curtain in the same velvet stroke, and the bakery, the warm whitewashed bakery where she had grown up inside her mother's love shaped like bread, was suddenly full of the roar of a thing she had called magic and called shame and never once, until that instant, called by what it was.

"Vex!" Her mother was awake, was on her feet, was pulling her back from the burning bed by the shoulders, sobbing, her grey face lit orange and terrible. "Vex, stop, stop, the house —"

Vex could not stop. That was the terror of it, the true terror, the one that would come back to her in the oubliette on the nights the scratching did not come: she wanted to stop, she was trying to stop, and the fire did not care. It was not her will anymore, or it was her will past all leash, the wanting and the grief and the stolen water and the six years and the closed doors all banked so long that when the sluice opened there was no closing it. The flame raced up the wall toward the beams, blackening the ceiling, and through the roar she heard her mother's voice and did not know it, and then she felt herself pulled backwards across the floor, her palms scraping, and her mother threw the flour sacks onto the burning bed one after another, smothering, smothering, until the roar choked into a sodden hiss and the only light left was the shrine candle, burning small and permitted in its glass, as if nothing had happened.

The bakery stank of smoke and charred straw. The ceiling was black. The curtains were gone.

And Marnie lay on the ruined pallet, and the fire had spared her — the fire had spared her, had burned the bed around her and the curtain beside her and had not touched the small body, as if even the beast had known not to take her again, as if her death belonged to the Flux and not to it, as if it wanted Vex to understand that it had not done this, that it had only ever done this.

Vex's mother held her on the floor of the bakery and sobbed into her hair, and Vex lay in her mother's arms with her palms raw from scraping and her chest full of a living heat and did not weep. That was the thing she would remember about the funeral: that she did not weep.

The funeral was silent.

The bell that should have rung for Marnie, six years old, daughter of the bakery, had been requisitioned for holy use, or so the sexton said, and the truth was the lower districts had buried so many children that week that the bell had worn out its sorrow. The mourners were few: the baker's widow in her one black shawl, the women of the lane who had come because a child's funeral was the one social debt even the starving could not refuse, and Vex, standing apart with her hands buried in her sleeves, holding the heat in her palms the way she had once hidden it from the Order, because she had discovered that the heat was all she had left of Marnie and she could not let it go.

They lowered the small coffin into the dry earth. The dust went down like water poured into a thirsty mouth. The priest said the words over the grave — dust to dust, flame to flame, the Chastened Flame refines what it burns — and Vex listened to the doctrine that had starved her sister and did not weep, because weeping was a door she had stopped being able to open, and instead she felt the heat pool in her chest like a living thing, patient as the drip, patient as a coal.

Her mother wept. The women of the lane wept. The priest wept, or performed weeping, which for the Order was the same thing. And Vex stood at the grave of her sister with the dry earth under her feet and the heat in her chest and the new knowledge sitting in her like a stone: the law is on the side of the owners of water. The Founders' healers served the rich while the children of the warrens died. The cisterns were locked. The healer's door was shut. And the city had buried her sister in silence, in dry earth, without a bell, because her sister's death was not a story the city wanted to tell.

That night the Founders' banquet music floated over the walls.

Vex sat on the bakery roof — she had climbed out the loft window, the way she had climbed it as a child to watch the stars with Marnie — and looked down at the Founders' Quarter, lit up gold and oblivious, and listened to the strings and the horns and the waltz that had played over Marnie's death rattle and over her grave, and she felt the heat in her chest rise into her hands and lie there, waiting, no longer a shame but a fact, no longer a coal but a furnace taking shape.

Something in her, the girl who had hidden her palms from the Order and dreamed of burning away injustice and never whispered it aloud, ended that night. Not died — the fire could not die, she had learned its law, it fed on the dead — but ended, the way a childhood ends, all at once, at a known hour, with a door.

Vex sat on the roof of the bakery in the sixth year of the dry season with her sister in the ground and the Founders dancing, and she did not speak the resolution aloud. It was not yet a plan. But she looked at the gold-lit quarter where the owners of water slept well, and she felt the shape of her life turn under her like a wheel finding its axle, and she knew that the girl who had watched the stars with Marnie had gone down into the ground with her, and that something else — something that had been banked under wet cloths and prayers and staying small, something the Order had named heresy and her mother had named risk and Thistle had named a door waiting to break — had taken her place.

She pressed her open palms flat against the warm tiles of the roof, and the heat came up through them, blackening nothing, burning nothing, just waiting, a beast that had come when she called it and stayed when she had not, and she let it wait.

The memory broke there, the way memories broke, and Vex lay on the cold stone of the oubliette with the drip going on and the dark pressing in, and she was shaking. She had not wept in the memory — could not weep, in the memory, had built that not-weeping into the foundation of everything she had become — but she was shaking now on the stone, her hands pressed flat against the floor, the heat in her palms stirred and waking and answering her grief like a dog answering a whistle, and she made herself breathe.

She counted the stones. She recited her mother's prayer until it broke in her mouth. She said Marnie's name aloud, once, quietly, the way you say a name to wake someone, and the dark held it, and no one answered, and she said it again.

The heat in her palms settled, slowly, the way it always did when she refused to feed it. She had learned the hunger. She had learned that the fire came for her grief and she could meet it with refusal, could meet it with the row of stones, could meet it with the simple terrible work of carrying the dead whole instead of burning them. She lay in the dark and held the night of the wake with both hands — the slack fingers, the fixed fearless eyes, the bell that would not ring, the dry earth, the waltz — and she did not justify it and she did not excuse it and she did not feed the coal, and she let Marnie be dead, and herself be the one who had let it happen, and the wanting be what it was.

Dawn of the thirty-fifth day paled down the light shaft. Vex crawled to the water channel and set down the thirty-fifth stone, adding it to the row with her raw fingers. Thirty-five stones. The bowls still stood untouched in the corner; the hunger was a presence in her, patient as the drip, and she let it be there, because the choice was hers and it was the one thing in the cell that was hers, and she had learned, holding her sister's dying hand, exactly how much a life was worth of what a city could withhold.

She lay back on the stone. The dark held its breath. Somewhere behind the loose block, the woman who had promised to come back was digging — patient, careful, against the arithmetic of the city — and Vex let the thought of her lie beside the memory of Marnie's fixed fearless eyes, and found, to her own surprise, that they could share the dark.

"Not tonight," she whispered to the heat in her palms. "Not for this."

And the heat, for the first time in all her life, obeyed her when she asked it to wait — or she imagined it did, which in the oubliette, where the only proof of anything was the keeping of a promise, was nearly the same thing.

The waltz played on, somewhere above, in a city that did not know her name. And Vex lay in the tear-shaped cell and carried her sister out of the ground and into the row of stones, and did not weep, and did not forget, and waited for whatever was coming to come.

You always fix it.').
