Brother Cole asked what the completed stack was called; Sorrel answered 'The Cataclysm. A true history,' and he said 'Then let's give it to the city.' The Low Light network carried it: the ferryman took the first copy upriver in the grain barge before the bells and it came back with letters from the hills; the dyer's cellar shelved the chronicle above the reading tables where cloth once bled color (a woman in a dyer's apron read the banquet-menu chapter aloud twice so the children would hear); the undertaker's shop set a copy beside the door; and at the bread lines, the fountains, and the steps of the Sanctum the city read itself aloud in the daylight, correcting one another and adding their own names to the margins until the history was the city's own — assembled in public, held in public, no longer one woman's telling.

Sorrel's chronicle ('The Cataclysm: A True History') is now the city's shared history, read aloud and corrected in public, with copies upriver and letters coming back from the hills; Sorrel has begun the next page and the chronicle is not finished — it has only begun to be true. This ongoing chronicle, and Sorrel's continuing gathering of names and witnesses, must carry into the later chapters (the Garden of Ashes transformation of the Founders' Quarter and the Mirror Monument of the final chapter), so the city's memory keeps the fire and the names alive rather than closing the wound.

Per the chronicle's promise and Sorrel's oath, Sorrel must eventually see the sea for Thistle — the sea Thistle dreamed of where water falls from the sky for free — and carry Thistle's memory there; this is the unfulfilled promise woven through her chronicle work and must be honored in a later chapter.

chapters.name: The Garden of Ashes
chapters.content:
They argued about the Quarter for the whole of one grey winter — whether to raise the Founders' houses again from their own cellars, or to pave the ground over and forget, or to leave the ash alone as a monument to what fire does when it is handed to grief. The city argued in the reading rooms, in the margins of the chronicle, at the bread lines and the fountains, and in the end the argument settled into something no one had proposed and everyone recognized: not to rebuild, and not to forget, but to garden.

So the palaces' stones were broken, and that was the first honest thing done with them in a hundred years.

Fern arrived before first light with the stone crew, because the stone crew was hers to lead now, and she had never led anything in her life except her own hunger. She had sold her wedding ring for one bucket of brown water at the east well, in the sixth year of the dry season, and the clerk had weighed the gold and given her the bucket and not met her eyes, and she had carried it home to children who were already too weak to fight over it. She did not tell the crew this. She did not need to. Half of them had sold something. The Quarter's broken stones did not care what they had sold.

They worked the great gilded gates first, the ones that had carried ORDER AND ABUNDANCE in letters taller than a man. The fire had blackened them and the winter had rusted them, and the crew pried the letters off one by one, and the letters came away easily now, as if they had only ever been nailed on, which in a way they had. A boy named for the dead carried the O to the forge to be melted into something else. No one asked what. The gates themselves were not thrown away. They were lifted down and set as the garden's own gate, wider than the old one, swung open at both leaves so that nothing in the Quarter was behind a gate anymore, and children ran through it on the first morning the hinges were hung, and the whole city heard them and thought, slowly, of letting the Quarter be entered.

Fern broke the stones into path stones. It was a palace stone — she had seen the lintel over a Founder's door before the fire, carved with grapes and sheaves, the harvest made of other people's work. Now she struck it with a hammer and it split along the grain of its own weight, and she and a man whose name she was still learning carried the two halves to the path that would lead to the cistern, and set them in the turned earth, and tamped them. The path grew. It was not a Founders' way, wide enough for a procession of carts and priests. It was a garden path, one stone wide, the kind a body makes by walking the same way twice.

At the second bell the weary guard came down the path with a bucket of water for the crew, and Fern looked at him, and she knew him the way the whole city knew him now — the man who had said Eat through a door for forty-two days, the man who had stood with the keys behind the garrison commander on the pale morning the paper came for Aldous Vane. For forty-two days he had been the guard who said Eat. The garden gave him back his name. Alder, he wrote it in the cistern rotation book that morning, in the blank space under his own thumbprint, and Fern saw him look at the letters afterward as if they belonged to someone else, and she said nothing, because saying nothing was also a kind of welcome.

The cistern stood in the middle of the Quarter, where the Founders' central court had been, and it was the thing the whole garden had been built around. It had been locked for a hundred years behind an iron gate while the water it held ran cold and unused and the lower districts bought their own water back at scarcity prices. The fire had gutted the gate. The city had kept the cistern, and cleaned it, and made it public, and now it was guarded not by men with pikes but by ordinary citizens on a rotation that everyone on the street could read on the board: the dyer, the undertaker's niece, the old tin-cup man, the woman in the green dress who had been first to touch the pillar's stone. Fern's name was on the board for the noon watch, and she stood at the cistern's rim at noon with her hand on the pump, and the water came up clear and cold, and children held out cups and tin bowls and a girl held out her hands cupped together, and Fern filled the girl's hands, and the girl drank and laughed and ran back to the others, and Fern stood at the rim a long moment with the empty bucket, remembering the weight of one bucket of brown water and the ring that had paid for it, and she did not know whether to weep, so she filled the bucket again for the new flowers, and the water ran free.

The flowers. That was the work that would take years and was already years old. The ash had been the first soil — the deep grey blanket of it, warm even in winter, holding everything that had burned. In the spring the wildflowers had come up on their own, poppies and dock and the small tough things that grow where fire has been, and the city had let them, and then had begun to plant around them. The paths turned between beds. The ruined walls were not torn down; they were left as holding walls, and roses climbed them. The great houses' footprints became gardens, each room a bed — the kitchen garden where the cook's boy had slept above the ovens, the laundress's yard where the wash lines had hung, now trellised with beans and morning glories. The stables' floor was a meadow. And along every path they planted rowans, the trees that survive dry years by sinking their roots deep, and a child asked why rowans, and an old woman said, because a girl who wanted to live was going to be called Rowan, and the child said, who was she, and the old woman said, no one yet. Which was not an answer, and was also the truest answer the garden had.

Poppy was the old flower-seller who had stood at the gilded gates for forty years with a basket, selling the Founders' processions a bit of color, and she had seen the smoking-hands girl pass in the moonlight on the night of the fire, and she had been sorry she had nothing to sell her. She told this story now, whenever she was asked, and she was asked often, because she was one of the elderly former servants whose stories were listened to at last, and because the telling had become a kind of work the city needed done. She told it true: that the girl had been thin and calm and terrible, that her hands had smoked in the moonlight like banked coals, that Poppy had thought she was a ghost, that she had not been a ghost, that she had been a baker's daughter with a dead sister and a heart full of fire, and that Poppy had nothing to sell her, and the girl had not wanted anything anyway, only the gates down.

It was Poppy who took the children to the white street at noon, where the white house had stood, where the brick balcony had been. The balcony's bricks had been gathered and laid flat, and a flower box had been rebuilt on top of them, and in it grew red flowers, the same red as the dead stems the child had climbed onto to watch the fire. Children played there. That was the whole of the garden's answer to the worst thing — that children played there, that the swing hung again from a beam that had survived, that a boy pumped his legs and rose into the air above the spot where a small figure in a white dress had raised her hand to be saved. Poppy told the children the story in the way they could carry it: that a little girl had watched a bright thing and had not been afraid, and that a woman who carried fire in her hands had wanted to save her and could not, and that the woman had carried the little girl's name in her heart for the rest of her life, even though she never knew it, and the garden was what that carried name had grown into. The children listened the way children listen — half there, half already playing — and one of them, a girl with her hair in a ragged braid, stopped swinging long enough to say, so the fire is why the flowers are red, and Poppy said, something like that, and the girl said, I like the flowers, and went back to the swing, and Poppy stood with her hand on the flower box and let the tears come, because no one had ever told her the ending could be that.

At dusk the garden turned toward the graves. They lay at the garden's far end, where the old servants' wing had been, in a green bowl of ground between the cistern and the new rowans: the graves of servants and Founders lying together under a blanket of wildflowers, and no wall between them, and no mark of rank, only names and the years they had lived and the gaps where the names were lost standing like holes in a ledger. The cook's boy's mother came every evening with the cap on her knees and told him about the day, and the laundress's sister came with a copy of the chronicle and read the chapter about the fire aloud, softly, to the wildflowers, so that her sister's name would be said at least once before the dark. Fern came and knelt by the grave of the ring she had sold, which was not a grave at all, and laid her open hand flat on the grass, the way the woman in the green dress had laid hers on the pyre's stone.

Sorrel came down the path as the light went amber, and she was not carrying the chronicle — she was carrying the next page of it, a single sheet, still wet in the middle where the ink had not dried. She knelt at the edge of the graves and read aloud, and it was not a chapter; it was a list of the names the margins had given back that week, the names that had been missing, the ones the smoke could not write. She read them into the evening the way a gardener waters, one name at a time. And then she read the line she had written at the bottom, in the same hand that had written the dedication: that the garden was not a monument to close the wound but soil, and soil is what the dead become so that something can grow, and the growing is the only answer the city has that does not lie.

The youngest priest came at last light and knelt at the edge of the green bowl, a long way off from the graves, with his hands flat on the grass, and no one moved him, and no one stared. He had helped copy the pamphlet in a trembling hand; he had knelt through the burning; he had read Vane's name in the ember and understood what his blessing had been for. He did not speak. He did not pray in the Order's words. He sat very still, and the garden held him the way it held everyone, and after a while he said, in a voice that cracked, flame that feeds, flame that warms, flame that burns only what is given it — the prayer that had been a child's binding and a woman's last word, the prayer Sorrel had written into the chronicle so the city could learn it — and the words held, whole and unbroken, and the grass was wet under him, and no one said anything, and that was the prayer, said over the graves of both sides, given freely at last.

The first rain came as the lanterns were being lit — a soft one, the kind the dry years had forgotten, falling out of a sky that had no business with rain. It fell on the red flowers, on the swing, on the rowans, on the path stones Fern had set that morning, on the graves under the wildflowers, and the city stood in it, and the children ran in it with their mouths open, and Poppy said, to no one, water falling from the sky for free, and Sorrel heard her, and touched the rowan sapling beside her, and said nothing, because the sea was still a promise she had not yet kept, but the rain was a beginning of it, and a beginning was more than she had had that morning.

Fern stood at the cistern's rim in the rain, and she thought of the ring, and of the bucket of brown water, and of the girl who had cupped her hands at noon, and she put her hand on the pump, and she did not know whether to weep, so she let the rain do it, and the rain did, and the water ran free.

The garden held the night then. The lanterns burned along the paths. Somewhere beyond the wall, at the pillar in the Sanctum square, the shrine kept its own vigil, the paper boats still sailing the drawn wave, the charred words still traced with fresh ash, and the two places — the shrine where a woman had burned reading, and the garden where a city was learning to grow — were the same country now, one the wound and one the healing, and no wall between them.

That was the day, and the day was not finished, because the work was the kind that is never finished: the paths would be walked, the cistern would be guarded, the names would keep coming back from the margins, the stories would keep being told, and Vex's name would be spoken in the garden the way it was spoken nowhere else in Meridian — not as heroine, not as curse, but as the costly ancestor who had refused to let the city look away, and who had paid, with everything she was, for the ground the wildflowers grew in. The garden did not say she was forgiven. The garden did not say she was innocent. The garden said her name, and watered the red flowers, and went on with the slow work of turning ashes into soil.

set.name: Vex
set.description: DEAD — consumed on the 42nd morning; ash scattered on smoke, her final smoke-written words charred into the Sanctum pavement. In the Garden of Ashes (the transformed Founders' Quarter) her name is spoken as it is nowhere else in Meridian: not as heroine, not as curse, but as 'the costly ancestor who refused to let the city look away' — the garden does not say she was forgiven and does not say she was innocent; it says her name, waters the red flowers on the white street, and goes on with the slow work of turning ashes into soil. Her full story lives in Sorrel's chronicle ('The Cataclysm: A True History'), now the city's own shared history, read aloud and corrected in public; her charcoal note ('Don't revolt. Bear witness. Publish everything. But do not let them forget their own fire.') is folded in Sorrel's shift against her heart, and her words 'You are my mirror' are a saying across the districts.

set.name: Sorrel
set.description: Thistle's sister, of the Low Light, chronicler of the Cataclysm. Her completed chronicle — 'The Cataclysm: A True History,' dedicated 'For Marnie and Thistle — the two sisters who lit a city' — has been given to the city through the Low Light network and is read aloud, corrected, and margined with new names everywhere; she continues the gathering. In the Garden of Ashes at dusk she carried the next page of the chronicle to the green bowl of graves and read aloud the names the margins had given back that week (the ones the smoke could not write), one name at a time like a gardener watering, and wrote that the garden is not a monument to close the wound but soil, and soil is what the dead become so that something can grow, and the growing is the only answer that does not lie. In the first rain she heard Poppy say 'water falling from the sky for free' and touched the rowan sapling beside her and said nothing — the sea for Thistle is still a promise not yet kept, only begun. She keeps Vex's charcoal note against her heart, the oilcloth evidence bundle, the ember brand in the Undercroft cistern hall, and the endless work of the next page. Emotional condition: grief intact, terrible patience, strange calm that the seeing is not done and will never be done.

set.name: youngest priest
set.description: The young priest of the Order who recited the Chastened Flame blessing over Vex on the 42nd morning, saw the incense smoke part around her, read Vane's name in the ember and understood what his blessing had been for. In the weeks after he helped copy a pamphlet in a trembling hand, knelt at the shrine's candlelight with the censer cold while the white row stood far off. In the Garden of Ashes at last light he knelt at the edge of the green bowl of graves, a long way off, hands flat on the grass, and said aloud, in a voice that cracked, the mother's prayer — 'flame that feeds, flame that warms, flame that burns only what is given it' — the words holding whole and unbroken over the graves of both sides, and the grass was wet under him. He is the seed of the Order's reckoning and its slow, inch-by-inch distancing from the deposed Governor.

set.name: Alder (the weary guard)
set.description: The formerly unnamed guard who guarded the oubliette for forty-two days, said 'Eat,' left the jug of water, gave Vex the festival bread, folded a Low Light paper into his tunic, and stood with the keys behind the garrison commander at Aldous Vane's arrest. In the Garden of Ashes the garden gave him back his name: Alder, which he wrote in the cistern rotation book in the blank space under his own thumbprint on the day the stone crew broke the Founders' gates' stones into paths, and he looked at the letters as if they belonged to someone else. He brought a bucket of water down the garden path to the crew at second bell; no longer the guard who said Eat but a citizen of the city whose water now runs free. He is the symbol of the ordinary men who turned, deniably, one small refusal at a time.

set.name: Fern
set.description: The mother who sold her wedding ring for one bucket of brown water at the east well in the sixth year of the dry season (she does not tell the stone crew this; half of them had sold something). Now she leads the stone crew in the Garden of Ashes that breaks the Founders' palaces' stones into garden path stones — she split the grape-and-sheaves lintel and carried the halves with a man whose name she is still learning to set the path to the cistern. She guards the cistern on the noon rotation (her name on the public board) and filled a girl's cupped hands with clean water at noon and stood a long moment with the empty bucket, remembering the weight of one bucket of brown water and the ring that paid for it, not knowing whether to weep. She kneels at the green bowl of graves in the evening, lays her open hand flat on the grass. In the first rain she stood at the cistern's rim, put her hand on the pump, let the rain do the weeping, and the water ran free. Has children who were too weak to fight over water in the dry years.

set.name: Poppy
set.description: The old flower-seller who stood at the gilded Founders' gates for forty years selling the processions a bit of color, and on the night of the Cataclysm saw the smoking-hands girl pass in the moonlight — thin, calm, terrible, hands smoking like banked coals — and was sorry she had nothing to sell her. Now one of the elderly former servants of the Founders' Quarter whose stories are listened to at last; she tells the true story whenever asked, a kind of work the city needs done. At noon she takes the children to the white street where the white house and brick balcony stood, where the balcony's gathered bricks lie flat under a rebuilt flower box of red flowers (the same red as the dead stems the Foundling child climbed onto to watch the fire), and tells the children a story they can carry: a little girl watched a bright thing and was not afraid, a woman who carried fire in her hands wanted to save her and could not and carried her name in her heart forever without ever knowing it, and the garden is what that carried name grew into; a child said 'so the fire is why the flowers are red,' and Poppy said 'something like that,' and let the tears come. In the first rain she said, to no one, 'water falling from the sky for free.'

After a grey winter of argument, Meridian transformed the Founders' Quarter not by rebuilding and not by paving over, but by gardening. The palaces' stones were broken into garden paths; the great gilded gates (ORDER AND ABUNDANCE letters pried off one by one and melted down) were kept and hung open at both leaves as the garden's own wide gate, behind nothing anymore, so children ran through on the first morning the hinges were hung. The cistern was kept, cleaned, made public, and guarded by ordinary citizens on a public rotation board (dyer, undertaker's niece, old tin-cup man, the woman in the green dress who was first to touch the pillar's stone). The ruined walls were left as holding walls for roses; the great houses' footprints became gardens, each room a bed; the stables' floor became a meadow; rowans were planted along every path. The graves of servants and Founders lie together in a green bowl of ground where the servants' wing was, under a blanket of wildflowers, no wall between them, no mark of rank, only names and years and gaps where names were lost.

Fern — the mother who sold her wedding ring for one bucket of brown water at the east well in the sixth year of the dry season — leads the stone crew of the Garden of Ashes, broke the Founders' lintel stones into path stones, guards the cistern on the noon rotation, and filled a girl's cupped hands with clean water at noon.

In the Garden of Ashes the garden gave the weary unnamed guard back his name: Alder, which he wrote in the cistern rotation book in the blank space under his own thumbprint the day the stone crew broke the gates' stones into paths; he also carried a bucket of water down the path to the crew at second bell.

Poppy, the old flower-seller who saw the smoking-hands girl pass in the moonlight on the night of the Cataclysm, took the children to the white street at noon, where the brick balcony's gathered bricks lie flat under a rebuilt flower box of red flowers (the red of the dead stems the Foundling child climbed onto), and told the story of the little girl who watched a bright thing and was not afraid and the woman who carried fire and could not save her and carried the girl's name in her heart forever; a child said 'so the fire is why the flowers are red,' and Poppy said 'something like that' and let the tears come.

At dusk in the Garden of Ashes, Sorrel knelt at the edge of the green bowl of graves and read aloud the next page of the chronicle — not a chapter but a list of the names the margins had given back that week, the names that had been missing, the ones the smoke could not write — one name at a time like a gardener watering, and read the line that the garden is not a monument to close the wound but soil, and soil is what the dead become so that something can grow, and the growing is the only answer that does not lie.

At last light in the Garden of Ashes, the youngest priest knelt at the edge of the green bowl of graves, a long way off, hands flat on the grass, and said in a cracking voice the mother's prayer — 'flame that feeds, flame that warms, flame that burns only what is given it' — the words holding whole and unbroken over the graves of both sides, the grass wet under him, no one moving him, no one staring.

The first rain fell on the Garden of Ashes as the lanterns were lit — soft, the kind the dry years had forgotten — falling on the red flowers, the swing, the rowans, the path stones, the graves under the wildflowers; the city stood in it, children ran in it with their mouths open, Poppy said to no one 'water falling from the sky for free,' and Sorrel touched the rowan sapling and said nothing — the sea for Thistle still a promise not yet kept, but a beginning.

In the Garden of Ashes, Vex's name is spoken as it is spoken nowhere else in Meridian: not as heroine, not as curse, but as the costly ancestor who refused to let the city look away and who paid, with everything she was, for the ground the wildflowers grow in — the garden does not say she was forgiven and does not say she was innocent; it says her name and waters the red flowers.

The Garden of Ashes — the public cistern guarded by the citizen rotation board, the path stones broken from the Founders' palaces, the graves of servants and Founders lying together under wildflowers in the green bowl, the rowans along every path, and the red flower box on the white street where children play where the Foundling died — must endure into the final chapter as the living transformation of the Founders' Quarter, standing in relation to the Mirror Monument (which rises where the pyre once burned) and the annual vigil; the garden and the shrine are the same country, one the wound and one the healing, with no wall between them.

chapters.name: The Mirror Monument
chapters.content:
They argued for a year about what should stand where the pyre had burned — in the reading rooms, in the margins of the chronicle, at the bread lines and the fountains — and in the end the argument settled into something no one had proposed and everyone recognized, because the city had learned the trick of it by then: not to raise a statue, and not to leave the ground empty, but to hold up a mirror.

So they cast her in bronze. The longest argument was whether she should have a name. Half the city wanted her name on it — the costly ancestor, the woman who had burned reading. The other half said a name would be a verdict, and she had spent her last hour refusing verdicts, and the city had spent the years since learning not to hand them out so easily. In the end they cast her nameless, and the namelessness was the truest thing about her: she had carried in her heart a child whose name she never knew, and had died with the names of the unknown on her lips, and the monument owed her the same honor — to stand for the one name and for all the names, the ones the smoke could write and the gaps where the names were lost.

She was a woman made of flame. The bronze rose from the stone heart of the old pyre, where the pillar had stood, the circle where the heat had once refused to touch her, and she leaned into a wind of her own making, hands open at her sides, and in her raised hands she held a mirror — not a real mirror, a great sheet of polished bronze, tall as a door, curved slightly, so that whoever stood before it saw themselves whole, framed in flame. The sculptor had been a woman from the dyer's cellar who had read the chronicle until she knew it by heart, and she had built the flame so that it moved around the mirror, and the people who stood before it were always standing at the heart of a fire that was their own reflection.

At the base, cut deep so that rain filled the letters and winter held ice in them, so that every child who learned to read learned this first, stood the question:

WHO LIT THE FIRST SPARK?

It was not her name. It was not a verdict. It was the question the city had learned to stand inside, and it was never finished, because the answer changed with whoever stood in the mirror.

The first vigil was held on the first morning of the harvest month, the anniversary of the burning, because the city would not let the day pass as a holiday and would not let it pass as nothing. No booths, no banners, no horn. At first light the ordinary citizens came — the same hands that guarded the cistern: the dyer, the undertaker's niece, the old tin-cup man, the woman in the green dress, grown older now, who had been first to touch the pillar's stone — and they polished the mirror. That was the rite, and it took the morning, because the bronze was tall as a door and the polishing had to be done by hand, in silence, the way the path stones had been set and the names read. When the mirror was bright enough to show a face, they stood back, and the city came.

Fern came, older now, the stone crew years behind her but the cistern rotation still her own, and she stood at the mirror and saw the woman she had become — the one who had sold a ring for a bucket and led a crew and filled a girl's cupped hands with clean water at noon, every noon, for years. She had thought, the first year, that the mirror would show her the ring. It showed her the hands. She laid her open palm flat on the bronze, the way she laid it on the grass by the graves, and went to stand by the cistern, where the water ran free.

Poppy came with the children, because telling the children was her work and the vigil was the telling made yearly. She told the story again, the way she had told it on the white street: the thin calm girl with the smoking hands, the little girl in the white dress who watched a bright thing and was not afraid, the woman who could not save her and carried her name in her heart forever. And she told them the new part — that the woman stood in flame holding a mirror, and the mirror was for them, and the question at the bottom was theirs to answer, and answering it was the whole of the grown-up work they were growing toward. A boy with a rowan leaf in his hair said, "But who was she?" and Poppy said, "Look," and the boy looked, and saw himself, and said, "That's me," and Poppy said, "Yes. That's the answer."

Alder came, and he did not stand in front of the mirror. He stood beside it, where the guards had stood, and watched the people look. He was old now, grey, his back still straight from the door he had stood at for forty-two days, and he no longer startled at his own name. He set a bucket down by the monument's base, old habit, or the garden's habit, which had become the same thing, and he thought of the woman he had said Eat to through a door, and of the bread he had given her on the morning of the burning, and of the paper he had folded into his tunic against his heart, and he stood his watch over the mirror the way he had stood his watch over the cell — and this time the watch was for everyone looking in, and that was the difference, and he knew it.

The youngest priest came — not young anymore, the censer years behind him, the Order's reckoning moved through him and out of him into the white row — and at the vigil he stood where the dais had been, and he waited until the reading was done, and then he said the prayer aloud, in the voice that had first cracked over it in the garden: flame that feeds, flame that warms, flame that burns only what is given it. The words held, as they had held for years, and the city said them with him, the whole square, because the prayer had become the city's own — the mother's prayer, learned from the chronicle, given back to the Order, given back to the city, belonging now to whoever said it over whoever they loved.

Then the reading. That was the heart of the vigil, and it was Sorrel's work, and she was older now — grey in the wet-straw hair that had been the color of the girl she had dug toward for a year. The note was still folded against her heart, in the same shift, the charcoal smudged and soft, and she read it to herself every year before she climbed the steps: Don't revolt. Bear witness. Publish everything. But do not let them forget their own fire. She had kept it. The city had kept it. The forgetting had stopped happening.

She climbed the steps with the chronicle in her arms — the same chronicle, the true history, worn, rebound twice, its margins full of the names the city had added over the years — and she read the names. All of them. Thistle, and Corin, and Corin's sister, and the Foundling child in the white dress, and the laundress, and the cook's boy, and the servants, and the debtors whose ledgers burned, and Marnie, and Vex. She read the names the smoke could write and the names the margins had given back, one name at a time, the way a gardener waters. The square stood in the reading. That was the arithmetic the vigil kept — not the false arithmetic of ledgers, the one that always balances because you write both sides, but the true arithmetic of who lives and who dies, and how easily that arithmetic is rigged, and how the rigging is the sin. Every year the city stood in that arithmetic and looked at it, and every year the mirror showed them the ones who would do the rigging next if they did not watch themselves, and the vigil did not celebrate the fire and did not close the wound. It held the wound open in the light, the way the garden held it in the soil, and the two — the monument where a woman had burned reading, and the garden where a city had learned to grow — were the same country still, one the wound and one the healing, and no wall between them.

And then Sorrel laid the bouquet.

She had brought it from the garden, as she did every year: red flowers, the same red as the flower box on the white street, bound with a rowan sprig — the tree that survives dry years by sinking its roots deep, the tree that was going to be a woman's name. She laid it at the base, under the question, and knelt, and the square was silent, and she did not pray. She had never prayed, not once, in all the years — she had written instead, and the writing was her prayer, and the names were her prayer, and the sea was her prayer.

The sea. She had kept that promise too, the one that had taken her longest because it was Thistle's own. One spring she had walked out of the city in the grey hour before dawn, the way a different woman had walked out on a different night, and she had walked until the land ran out. She had stood at the edge of the sea with the chronicle in her arms and the note against her heart, and read the dedication into the wind — For Marnie and Thistle, the two sisters who lit a city — and waded in up to her knees, letting the water take her hem, the water that fell from the sky and ran to the sea for free, the water Thistle had dreamed of all her short life, and she had said aloud, to the sea, to the sky, to the sister who was in both of them now: We made it. We're here. I carried you the whole way. And that night she had written the last page of the chronicle, the page the city never read because it was not for the city — a single line: The sea for Thistle, at last. Water falling from the sky for free. It lay there still, between the dedication and the world, a promise kept in ink.

A child tugged at her sleeve.

It was a girl, eight or nine, hair in a ragged braid — the same ragged braid as the girl who had said so the fire is why the flowers are red, years ago in the garden, or a different child, the garden made them all a little alike. She had been watching the bronze woman for a long time, and now she asked the question the monument had been waiting for, the question that was never finished:

"Who was she?"

Sorrel looked from the girl to the bronze woman — the flame, the open hands, the mirror — and heard her own voice answering before she had decided to speak, the way the truth does:

"She was someone who couldn't bear a world where some decide who drinks," Sorrel said. "She tried to change it. She didn't know how well."

The girl considered this with the grave patience of the very young. "Did she?"

"Did she what?"

"Change it."

Sorrel looked at the cistern, where Fern stood with her hand on the pump and the water running free. She looked at the garden beyond the gate, at the rowans and the red flowers and the graves under the wildflowers. She looked at the square full of people who read the chronicle aloud and corrected one another and added their names to the margins, who came every year and stood in the mirror and let it show them the arithmetic. She gave the girl the answer that held both the true and the not-true:

"I don't know," she said. "That's the question."

The girl looked at the bronze woman again, and then — because the mirror was bright, and because she was a child, and because the monument had been built for exactly this — she stepped forward and looked into the polished bronze, into the flame that was her own reflection, and saw herself, whole, standing at the heart of a fire that was hers, and she did not look away.

Sorrel watched her. The girl's face in the mirror was young and unburned and full of wanting, and Sorrel knew the wanting — she had seen it in a baker's daughter's hands, in a scullery maid's laugh, in the whole of the city that had whispered its wish into the fire and then stood in the square pretending it had not. The girl would grow up in a city with open cisterns and a garden where the Founders' stones were paths, and she would still carry the wanting, because the wanting was not the fire — the wanting was the hunger, and the hunger was what the mirror showed, and the question was what they did with it. Whether they turned it into locked gates or open ones. Whether they decided who drank, or let the water run. Whether they lit the first spark in a child's white dress, or put the fire down and picked up the paper instead.

That was the arithmetic. That was the vigil. That was the monument.

And the city passed it every day, the way cities pass their monuments, on the way to the cistern and the garden and the bread and the work — a man carrying a bucket, a woman with a copy of the chronicle under her arm, children running to the swing, the old tin-cup man touching two fingers to his chest as he went by — and every day, in the polished bronze, they glimpsed themselves, and in themselves the fire they carried, the one that could feed or burn, warm or devour, depending on whose hands held it and whether the hands had learned to speak. They did not stop and stand before it every day. That would have been too much. But the glimpse was the thing, the quick daily sight of the flame in their own faces, and it was enough, and it was never done.

Justice was never a verdict handed down from above. The city had learned that at the pillar, where a woman had died giving back a verdict that was not hers to give and not theirs to take. It was a question. It stood in bronze at the heart of the square, in the mirror of a nameless woman made of flame, and every generation stood in front of it and answered it with their lives, and every generation was answered by the mirror, and the question did not end, because a question that can be answered once is a question that has stopped looking at faces, and this one never would.

The girl in the ragged braid stood in the mirror a long time. When she stepped back, she turned to Sorrel, and she did not ask who the woman was again. She asked the other question, the one the monument was built to receive, the one that would be hers to carry and hers to pass on, and her voice was small and clear in the morning air:

"Who lit the first spark?"

Sorrel looked at her, and at the bronze woman holding the mirror to the crowd, and she smiled the way the garden smiled — crooked and defiant and tired, full of the strange calm that the seeing was not done and would never be done — and she said:

"We all did. Every one of us, every day we chose the locked gate or the open one. That's why we have to keep looking."

The girl looked at her own reflection once more, and then she ran to the cistern, where the water ran free, and drank with her cupped hands, and laughed, and the laugh was quick and crooked and defiant, and somewhere in the bronze mirror the flame held the shape of a woman who had carried fire in her hands and a broken heart, and the shape was smiling, or it was not, but the mirror was bright, and the water ran free, and the question stood in the square, and the city answered it with its days.

set.name: Vex
set.description: DEAD — consumed on the 42nd morning; ash scattered on smoke. Years later she is remembered not as heroine or curse but as 'the costly ancestor who refused to let the city look away,' her name spoken in the Garden of Ashes as nowhere else in Meridian. Her story lives in Sorrel's chronicle ('The Cataclysm: A True History'), now the city's shared history, read aloud and corrected in public; her charcoal note ('Don't revolt. Bear witness. Publish everything. But do not let them forget their own fire.') is folded in Sorrel's shift against her heart. Her final words are charred into the Sanctum pavement where the shrine formed, and her image now stands at the heart of the square as the Mirror Monument: a nameless woman of bronze flame holding a polished bronze mirror to the crowd, with the question 'WHO LIT THE FIRST SPARK?' cut deep at the base — nameless because she carried in her heart a child whose name she never knew and died with the names of the unknown on her lips, so the monument stands for the one name and all the names, the ones the smoke could write and the gaps where the names were lost. She is the mirror every passerby glimpses their own fire in.

set.name: Sorrel
set.description: Thistle's sister, of the Low Light, chronicler of the Cataclysm. Now older, grey in the hair that was the color of the girl she dug toward for a year. She keeps the charcoal note folded against her heart in the same shift (smudged and soft now), and the oilcloth evidence bundle, and the ember brand's memory; the chronicle — 'The Cataclysm: A True History,' dedicated 'For Marnie and Thistle — the two sisters who lit a city' — has been rebound twice and its margins are full of the names the city added over the years. She fulfilled the sea promise one spring: walked out of the city in the grey hour before dawn, stood at the edge of the sea with the chronicle and the note, read the dedication into the wind, waded in to her knees letting the water take her hem, and said aloud to the sea and sky and her sister 'We made it. We're here. I carried you the whole way.' That night she wrote the last page of the chronicle, not for the city but for herself: 'The sea for Thistle, at last. Water falling from the sky for free.' At the annual vigil she climbs the steps with the chronicle in her arms and reads the names aloud, one at a time like a gardener watering — the names the smoke could write and the names the margins gave back — and then lays the bouquet at the monument's base: red flowers bound with a rowan sprig, brought from the garden. She does not pray; she writes, and the writing is her prayer, and the names are her prayer, and the sea is her prayer. She answers a child's question with 'She was someone who couldn't bear a world where some decide who drinks. She tried to change it. She didn't know how well' and, when asked who lit the first spark, answers 'We all did. Every one of us, every day we chose the locked gate or the open one.' Emotional condition: grief intact, terrible patience, strange calm that the seeing is not done and will never be done; the chronicle is finished and unfinished — it will never be finished, only begun to be true.

set.name: Aldous Vane
set.description: Former Governor of Meridian — DEPOSED and ARRESTED by his own guards on a pale gold morning in the weeks after the burning; the forgetting stopped happening around him and became a verdict. Held in the courthouse, stripped of office, undone by paper and public shame. By the years of the Mirror Monument his name is read aloud in the annual vigil's reading of Vane's ledgers (the shell companies Second Well, the Ashford Trust, Gull & Sons; the reopened water contracts; the grain speculation; the confectioner's bill paid from the emergency fund), and the monument's question — who lit the first spark — is understood in part as a standing answer to how the machine that decides who drinks finds a patient clerk like him. He is the past the city holds open in the light rather than closes over.

set.name: youngest priest
set.description: The young priest of the Order who recited the Chastened Flame blessing over Vex, saw the incense smoke part around her, read Vane's name in the ember, and understood what his blessing had been for. Not young anymore, the censer years behind him; the Order's reckoning moved through him and out of him into the white row. He knelt through the shrine's candlelight with the censer cold, said the mother's prayer over the graves in the Garden of Ashes in a cracking voice, and at the annual vigil stands where the dais had been, waits until the reading is done, and says the prayer aloud — 'flame that feeds, flame that warms, flame that burns only what is given it' — with the whole square saying it with him, the mother's prayer learned from the chronicle, given back to the Order, given back to the city.

set.name: Brother Cole
set.description: Apostate priest of the Low Light, older now, in the Undercroft cistern hall by the ember brand. He gave the chronicle to the city ('Then let's give it to the city'), continues organizing distribution along the map of districts, rations the granary, husbands the lamp room's flame. He laughed at the Order calling the pamphlets heresy — 'They're right. It is.' — and once called Vex 'a broken instrument that can still sing.' In the years of the Mirror Monument the paper revolution he helped kindle has become the city's shared history; the chronicle is rebound twice and read aloud and corrected in public.

set.name: Alder (the weary guard)
set.description: The guard who said 'Eat' for forty-two days, gave Vex the festival bread, folded a Low Light paper into his tunic, and stood with the keys at Vane's arrest. The garden gave him back his name, which he wrote in the cistern rotation book; now old, grey, his back still straight from the door he stood at for forty-two days, he no longer startles at his own name. At the annual vigil he stands beside the Mirror Monument rather than in front of it, where the guards once stood, and watches the people look — the watch he kept over the cell, but now the watch is for everyone looking in, and that is the difference, and he knows it.

set.name: Fern
set.description: The mother who sold her wedding ring for one bucket of brown water; she led the stone crew that broke the Founders' palaces into garden paths and guards the cistern on the noon rotation. Older now, the stone crew years behind her but the cistern rotation still her own. At the vigil she stands at the mirror and sees the woman she has become; she lays her open palm flat on the bronze the way she lays it on the grass by the graves, and goes to stand by the cistern where the water runs free.

set.name: Poppy
set.description: The old flower-seller who saw the smoking-hands girl pass in the moonlight; one of the elderly former servants whose stories are listened to at last. She brings the children to the vigil every year and tells the story — the thin calm girl with smoking hands, the little girl in the white dress who was not afraid, the woman who could not save her and carried her name in her heart forever — and the new part: that the woman stands in flame holding a mirror, that the mirror is for them, and that the question at the bottom is theirs to answer. To a child's 'who was she' she answers 'Look,' and the child sees himself, and she says 'Yes. That's the answer.'

set.name: The Foundling child (nameless)
set.description: The Foundling child, daughter of the High Justiciar, in the white dress, whose raised hand Vex carried into the flame. Her name was never known; the Mirror Monument is deliberately nameless in part because of her — the nameless bronze woman stands for the one name and all the names, the ones the smoke could write and the gaps where the names were lost. Her name, if it ever resurfaces, still stands to be returned to the margins of the chronicle and read over the graves.

Years after the burning, after a year of argument in the reading rooms and chronicle margins, Meridian raised the Mirror Monument where the pyre once burned: a woman of bronze flame holding a polished bronze mirror to the crowd, nameless, with 'WHO LIT THE FIRST SPARK?' cut deep at the base (so rain fills the letters and winter holds ice in them, and every child who learns to read learns this first). The sculptor was a woman from the dyer's cellar who knew the chronicle by heart; she built the flame to move around the mirror so those who stand before it stand at the heart of a fire that is their own reflection. Nameless by deliberate choice — half the city wanted her name, half said a name would be a verdict and she spent her last hour refusing verdicts; and because she carried a child's name she never knew and died with the names of the unknown on her lips, the monument stands for the one name and all the names.

The first vigil was held on the first morning of the harvest month, the anniversary of the burning — no booths, no banners, no horn. Ordinary citizens (the same hands that guard the cistern) polish the mirror by hand in silence as the rite; when it is bright enough to show a face they stand back and the city comes. Fern stands in the mirror and sees the woman she became; Poppy brings the children and tells the story and the new part (the mirror is for them, the question is theirs); Alder stands beside the monument where the guards stood and watches the people look; the priest says the mother's prayer with the whole square saying it with him; and the vigil's heart is the reading of the names by Sorrel from the chronicle — Thistle, Corin, Corin's sister, the Foundling child, the laundress, the cook's boy, the servants, the debtors, Marnie, Vex — one name at a time like a gardener watering, the names the smoke could write and the names the margins gave back. The vigil does not celebrate the fire and does not close the wound; it holds the wound open in the light and keeps the arithmetic of who lives and who dies and how easily it is rigged.

One spring Sorrel fulfilled the sea promise for Thistle: she walked out of the city in the grey hour before dawn the way a different woman walked out on a different night, and walked until the land ran out; she stood at the edge of the sea with the chronicle in her arms and Vex's note against her heart, read the dedication into the wind ('For Marnie and Thistle — the two sisters who lit a city'), waded in to her knees letting the water take her hem — the water that falls from the sky and runs to the sea for free, the water Thistle dreamed of all her short life — and said aloud to the sea, to the sky, to her sister in both of them: 'We made it. We're here. I carried you the whole way.' That night she wrote the last page of the chronicle, not for the city but for herself: 'The sea for Thistle, at last. Water falling from the sky for free.' The chronicle's sea promise is now kept; she keeps the note against her heart still.

At the annual vigil at the Mirror Monument, a girl of eight or nine with a ragged braid asked 'Who was she?' and Sorrel answered: 'She was someone who couldn't bear a world where some decide who drinks. She tried to change it. She didn't know how well.' Asked if she changed it, Sorrel answered 'I don't know. That's the question.' The girl stepped into the polished bronze and looked into the flame that was her own reflection and did not look away. Then she asked 'Who lit the first spark?' and Sorrel answered: 'We all did. Every one of us, every day we chose the locked gate or the open one. That's why we have to keep looking.' The girl ran to the cistern and drank with cupped hands and laughed a quick, crooked, defiant laugh. The city passes the monument daily and glimpses in the mirror the fire they carry themselves — the one that can feed or burn, warm or devour, depending on whose hands hold it and whether the hands have learned to speak.
